Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs made a blunter case, pointing out that Europe has a larger population, greater wealth and stronger military capacity than Russia. He said Europe needed more resolve to act on that advantage.

Separately, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has complained about limits on Ukraine’s use of Starshield, the military satellite network run by SpaceX and owned by Elon Musk. He said on Thursday that the military faced fresh restrictions, and on Friday said the problem had not been resolved. According to Zelenskyy, connections worked only when devices moved below about 161 kilometres per hour, which he said made it impossible to use interceptors against jet-powered Shahed drones. He said he had told his ministers to intensify contacts with Washington.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk limited the speeds at which Ukrainian equipment could remain linked to the network. Both Musk and Trump have denied throttling Ukrainian access. Musk later accused Ukraine of using the service for military purposes, while Trump said Musk had restored it. Ukraine first raised the Starshield issue last month, following a row between Zelenskyy and Trump over a US decision to allow more Russian diesel into world markets.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz urged Trump on Friday to avoid any surprises on Ukraine in dealings with Putin. Trump is expected to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin at an APEC summit in China next week. Merz said some in Europe worry the meeting could produce a “second Anchorage moment,” a reference to the Alaska summit between Trump and Putin last summer, which European officials see as favouring Moscow. He also argued that Europe need not negotiate a new security order with Russia, since one already exists.
items.cav: Kushner’s remarks are reported second-hand, and Russia’s denial comes through Zakharova’s comments to DPA and Russian state media. The Starshield dispute rests on Zelenskyy’s claims and a Wall Street Journal report, while Musk and Trump deny throttling Ukrainian access. The sources do not say what outcome the talks might produce or when they would begin.
items.op: Europe is right to demand a seat at any table deciding Ukraine’s future, but that seat only carries weight if the bloc speaks with one accountable voice. Ukraine’s access to critical communications should not hinge on decisions that are not clearly explained. Any deal must be transparent about its terms before anyone signs it.

items.t: EU leaders add Italy and Poland to Ukraine peace team and stop short of naming a single envoy
items.s: European Union leaders have assembled a joint negotiating group for talks on Ukraine but declined to appoint one envoy, leaving foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas without the role she sought. Whether Moscow will sit down with European representatives remains unclear.
p: Leaders meeting in Dublin on Friday at an informal summit settled on a combined group to speak for Europe in the Ukraine talks. France, Germany, Italy, Poland and Britain form the core, and representatives of the European Council, the European Commission and NATO will also take part.

The question of naming one special envoy took up much of the discussion. According to the report, Ukraine, the United States and even Russia had all urged the EU to pick a single representative, which makes the decision not to do so stand out.

Before the meeting, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni had complained about the disorder in the European voices on the peace process and pressed for a lone envoy. Instead, leaders widened the existing negotiating circle to take in Italy and Poland. Warsaw had earlier cautioned that Western European capitals should not make decisions on behalf of the East.

European Council President António Costa said Europe was fully behind the process and hoped it would produce concrete results. Pressed on Kallas's ambitions, he cited the EU treaties, arguing that the European Council president speaks for the bloc on common foreign and security matters at the level of leaders, while the Commission president's remit covers external matters tied to the Community.

Kallas argued that representing the bloc on foreign policy fell within her mandate, pointing to a 2024 leaders’ decision. She also conceded that Russians did not want her, which she attributed to her strong views. Ursula von der Leyen, who serves as a Commission vice-president, did not back her either, stressing that leaders choose who represents them. Merz said Berlin saw no need for an institutional debate at present and that the E3 format worked well with Italy and Poland included.

The arrangement mostly puts in writing a format the United States has already used while brokering the talks. The E3, EU institutions and NATO attended recent rounds in Miami, Oslo, Brussels and Abu Dhabi. Italy took part in the Abu Dhabi session, and Poland is expected to join the next round.

The open issue is whether Moscow will meet European negotiators face to face, something it has repeatedly refused to do. US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner travelled to Moscow on Thursday to press President Vladimir Putin. Afterwards, both said Russia had signalled it was willing to hold such talks, but the Kremlin downplayed this, so no meeting is assured.
items.cav: The claim that Moscow was willing to hold face-to-face talks comes from the US envoys and is not confirmed by the Kremlin, which downplayed it. The sources do not say when or where any such meeting could take place.
items.op: Europe's peace diplomacy will only carry weight if it speaks with a clear and accountable voice. Leaders chose to keep a committee of capitals rather than name one envoy, which avoids a fight over Kallas but leaves the mandate vague. Voters deserve to know who is negotiating in their name, and the EU should say so openly.

items.t: Microsoft 365 outage of over 22 hours spotlights reliance on a few tech firms
items.s: An outage at Microsoft that ran for more than 22 hours disrupted Outlook and other Microsoft 365 services, prompting questions about how much essential work depends on a small number of technology companies. Microsoft has apologised and attributes the problem to a technical fault rather than a cyber-attack.
p: According to the BBC, the disruption lasted more than 22 hours and left many users without access to Outlook and other Microsoft 365 tools. Commentators have used it to ask how far essential services lean on a few large technology firms.

The trigger, as described in the report, was a set of routine automated checks that switched some servers off. Fewer machines were left to carry the load, and the survivors were swamped with traffic. Engineers then brought systems back in stages, a process that took almost a full day.

The reach extended well beyond office email. Around 430 million people worldwide use Microsoft 365, and problems were logged in more than 70 countries. Email went down for the US House of Representatives and Australian intelligence agencies, while court systems in Singapore and airline support desks in India were also hit.

Flora Hamilton, executive director of the Small Business Charter, called the episode a “stark reminder” of how firms depend on digital tools. For small and medium-sized enterprises, she said, email underpins contact with customers and suppliers as well as their income.

Walter Pasquarelli, a strategist, told the BBC that the outage exposed the weak points and dependence of governments, companies and critical infrastructure. He suggested that failures of this kind could spread further as more tools are linked to email, calendars and files.

Gergely Orosz, a former software engineer at several large tech companies, said outages of this sort are not rare. What stood out to him was how long recovery took. He pointed to the world’s reliance on a few major US firms and proposed dividing services by region to limit the damage, a design he said Amazon already applies to its AWS cloud platform.

Microsoft has apologised and says the cause was a technical fault, not a cyber-attack. A spokesperson defended the slow return to service, saying the pace reflected the scale of demand and produced a more stable restoration. The company says it is examining what happened, and that its findings are meant to guide steps against a repeat.
The reporting does not set out what the review is expected to contain, and the explanation of the cause comes from Microsoft itself.
items.cav: The explanation of the cause is Microsoft’s own account, and the review has not been published. The impact figures and the list of affected institutions are as reported by the BBC and have not been independently verified here.
items.op: Critical digital infrastructure should not rest on a few companies without transparency. Microsoft owes customers, public bodies and courts a published post-incident review, not only an apology. Dependence is a policy choice, and it should be scrutinised as one.

items.t: Microsoft Outlook outage disrupts companies, schools and local governments across the US
items.s: A Microsoft Outlook outage that began on Thursday afternoon disrupted companies, schools and local governments across the United States. By Friday the service was recovering, but some officials said parts of their operations were still down.
p: The outage affected a range of Microsoft tools that organisations use for messaging, scheduling, video calls and file storage in the cloud. According to local leaders, the problems began around 1pm ET on Thursday. By Friday morning Outlook was coming back, but officials in cities and counties including Miami, Maryland and Los Angeles told residents that some staff and services remained out of reach.

In Arapahoe county, Colorado, a detention facility said it could not accept online bond payments, so people seeking immediate release had to pay in person at the jail until email was working again. The Los Angeles county sheriff’s department said its email and other communication platforms were disrupted. Emergency management offices in Fredericksburg and Gillespie county, Texas, said they could not receive emails and asked people to phone instead.

In Maryland, the Washington suburban sanitary commission, which supplies drinking water and treats sewage for parts of the state, warned that its technicians might be held up and that some customers could struggle to pay their water bills. In Washington, congressional staffers told Politico that the disruption was especially damaging during the lame duck session, as their offices were negotiating pending bills and preparing for the next Congress.

Schools were hit too. Districts in Richmond, Virginia, and Port Washington, New York, told parents on Friday morning that they had lost service and urged them to contact the school by phone or through other online education platforms. The Albany school district said its services had been restored. The Colorado School of Mines asked faculty to be lenient with deadlines, although many of its systems ran on Google Workspace and Canvas, which were not affected.

Developers Anthropic and OpenAI, whose products depend on Microsoft connections, also reported problems. Anthropic said it was seeing signs of recovery but that some users could still get errors. OpenAI said it was still looking into faults with “Microsoft connectors” that were slowing performance. Meanwhile, the industrial manufacturer Workhorse Group postponed its third-quarter earnings call, which had been planned for Thursday afternoon.

Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna said late on Thursday that he saw nothing suggesting the failure was caused by hacking or other cyber activity. On Friday the company reported better service availability, while cautioning that some users could still face intermittent access problems or delayed email as recovery continued. The sources reviewed do not identify a cause for the outage.
items.cav: The cause of the outage is not established in the sources. Lamanna’s statement that there was no sign of malicious activity is a company claim, and Microsoft’s description of recovery is its own assessment. Most of the local impacts are reported second-hand through statements from officials and organisations.
items.op: When one cloud provider can disrupt detention facilities, water utilities and schools at once, the public has a stake in how that dependence is managed. Microsoft should publish a clear account of what failed and which safeguards will change. Reassurance that no attack occurred is not a substitute for transparency.

items.t: Kremlin revives 2021 demands on Nato as it pushes for a new European security order
items.s: Vladimir Putin has put European security back at the centre of talks on Ukraine, and the BBC’s Russia editor reads the move as a win for Moscow. Kyiv’s European backers call it a trap that could delay a ceasefire.
p: Russian President Vladimir Putin says he wishes “eternal peace” for Ukraine. The BBC’s Russia Editor, Steve Rosenberg, points out that this is the same leader who ordered the full-scale invasion nearly five years ago and who still rejects a comprehensive ceasefire.

After talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, the Kremlin called for “a new, long-term architecture of indivisible security and peace.” Rosenberg translates the phrase as a plan to reshape Europe’s security arrangements in Russia’s favour. He describes it as potentially the biggest change to European security since the end of the Cold War.

The Kremlin has also returned to its draft treaties with the United States and Nato, first published in December 2021. Those proposals would have halted Nato’s eastward expansion, given Moscow guarantees that Ukraine and Georgia would never join, and rolled back alliance military infrastructure in central and eastern European countries that joined after the Soviet collapse. Western leaders rejected them as an unacceptable ultimatum, and Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine about two months later.

Yuri Ushakov, Putin’s foreign policy aide, has suggested Moscow may add “certain new considerations” to its demands, citing Western efforts to inflict a strategic defeat on Russia. Rosenberg notes that the Kremlin’s success so far is simply that European security is now part of the discussion. The Russian newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda argued that diplomats needed a second victory, forcing the West to take Russia’s concerns about Nato enlargement seriously.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has called Moscow’s demands a “trap” designed to shift attention away from a ceasefire. She argued that a ceasefire should come first, followed by a peace agreement, and only then discussions on Europe’s wider security architecture.

Witkoff said after his Moscow meetings that Putin had agreed to European representatives joining the next round of Ukraine peace talks. However, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Friday that no final decision had been taken. He said a wider format would depend on understanding European “true intentions” and their readiness to support the peace process.

Rosenberg adds that the Kremlin is negotiating from a position of confidence, with the United States seeking a deal and European leaders in contact with Moscow. Norway’s and Finland’s leaders recently called Putin. Russian media have also compared a possible meeting next week in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping to the Big Three meeting of 1945. Rosenberg says that Russia has suffered heavy battlefield losses and that Ukrainian drone strikes are hitting Russian oil refineries, raising fears of fuel shortages, but that none of this has yet persuaded Putin to end the fighting.
items.cav: The analysis is by the BBC’s Russia Editor, and the Kremlin’s intentions are reported through its statements and aides rather than confirmed negotiating terms. The Shenzhen meeting is described as possible, not scheduled, and the evidence gives no figures for Russian losses or fuel shortages.
items.op: Europe’s security cannot be rewritten through an old ultimatum dressed up as a peace plan. Any talk of new arrangements should follow a ceasefire and be conducted openly, with Ukraine and its European partners at the table. Moscow’s attempt to reopen 2021 demands should be treated as a bid for leverage, not a basis for negotiation.

items.t: Kallas warns EU against Russian ‘traps’ as Europe moves to name its negotiators for Ukraine talks
items.s: EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas accused Moscow of using a debate over European security to distract from its war, as leaders at a Dublin summit moved to settle who would speak for Europe.
p: Kaja Kallas said Moscow was seeking to open a discussion about European security so that attention moved away from its aggression. Speaking as she arrived at the summit in Dublin, she told EU partners not to fall into the trap she said Russia was laying, and described the conflict as one with a clear aggressor and a clear victim.

Russia has returned to demands for a sweeping overhaul of Europe’s security order. Those demands were turned down in 2021, when critics saw them as a threat to the sovereignty of countries in central and eastern Europe. The most recent round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the United States took place in Abu Dhabi this week.

Jared Kushner, the envoy and son-in-law of Donald Trump, said on Thursday night that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to widen the next round of peace negotiations to include Europeans. Moscow quickly disputed that. The Kremlin said it would consider an expanded format once it understood Europe’s true intentions, and its lead negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, said it was unclear what there was to discuss with Europe.

European governments have said they will back Ukraine in any negotiations but want a ceasefire first, and they point to a dense network of security agreements that Russia has broken. Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, said there was no need to discuss a European security architecture because one already exists, and that Germany could expect a seat in any European delegation. Ursula von der Leyen, the Commission president, argued that Europe’s presence would protect its interests and support Ukraine.

After the Dublin meeting, European Council president António Costa said leaders had agreed on a negotiating group made up of the EU institutions and the E5: Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland. He called for Europe to speak with a single, united voice.

The idea of such a grouping had taken shape over recent months, but pressure to formalise it grew after Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged his European partners to decide who would represent them. Kushner had mocked the lack of one person to speak for the continent. Paris and Berlin wanted their own envoys to keep a role in the E3 format, while smaller member states put more weight on Costa and Kallas.

Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, called the debate over representation “slightly overstated”, noting that member states have differing interests. He said some issues, such as financing Kyiv and Ukraine’s eventual EU membership, were purely EU matters, and that he was flexible on the format. Ireland’s taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said the UK and Norway each had a significant role. The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it was for the EU to decide who would represent the bloc.
Several leaders at the summit, including Kallas, stressed that Britain should be included, as a founder member of the coalition of the willing committed to future peacekeeping in Ukraine.
items.cav: The account rests on a single outlet’s reporting. Kushner’s claim about expanding the talks is second-hand and was disputed by Moscow, and the sources do not explain how the negotiating team will be finalised.
items.op: Europe has a fair claim to a seat at talks that will shape its security, and Moscow should not be allowed to set the agenda by reopening the wider order. A negotiating team earns credibility only when its mandate is public and its members can say whom they represent. A ceasefire and Ukraine’s future must come before any debate over the European architecture.

items.t: Microsoft outage disrupts email and Teams in at least 74 countries, from US courts to Japanese firms
items.s: A Microsoft 365 outage has affected organisations in at least 74 countries, with courts, city governments, hospitals and businesses reporting email and Teams problems. The company said services were recovering in several regions.
p: The disruption was detected after midday US Eastern Time on Thursday, which the BBC gave as 17:00 GMT. Microsoft said Outlook and Teams, along with its Copilot software, were experiencing “connectivity problems”. By 12:00 GMT on Friday, the company reported “encouraging recovery progress in Europe”, said Japan remained comparatively more stable and said North America was also improving.

In the United States, staff with the House of Representatives told Politico that their work had been halted. One House staffer described a lost day of legislative work without access to calendars and shared schedules. Courts from Los Angeles to Texas warned that communications might be delayed. The City of Austin said on X that its employees could not send or receive email, while its phone lines and 911 emergency services remained operational. Officials in several cities urged residents to call local offices instead of using email.

Workhorse Group, an electric truck maker, moved its third-quarter results from 12 November to 16 November, citing business disruptions linked to the outage. OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft services, which left some tools not working as expected.

In Canada, the public broadcaster CBC reported that a healthcare network running several Toronto hospitals had declared a code grey, an alert for infrastructure failure. The network, Unity Health Toronto, said its teams were having trouble sending and receiving email, but patient care was not affected.

In Japan, the Japan Times quoted an unnamed user saying that a firm had switched to fax for regular updates it usually sent as PDFs. Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki told reporters the government would continue to monitor the company’s response. In Singapore, officials said emergency services remained fully operational, while the courts urged people with urgent matters to telephone them. The Philippine Supreme Court warned that responses to emails and other transactions could be delayed.

In India, people in equity markets told BBC News they panicked when they could not reach daily research reports before their morning meeting. A senior executive at a large brokerage said, on condition of anonymity, that losing Teams was a challenge because most calls with big clients run on it.

Chinese firms rely largely on locally made software such as WPS Office, but the outage still caused frustration there, since Outlook is one of the few dependable channels for offices that work with overseas colleagues. Australia’s spy and federal police agencies were also affected, though officials suggested the impact was minimal.
items.cav: The sources do not give the cause of the outage or say when full service will be restored. The country count and recovery claims come from Microsoft’s own updates and have not been independently verified.
items.op: A single company’s failure has stalled courts, hospitals and legislators across the globe, which shows how much public business now depends on a few private platforms. Governments should publish clear dependency plans and explain what failed. Dependence without transparency is a risk that citizens are paying for.

items.t: Microsoft outage stretches past 18 hours as Outlook, Teams and Copilot remain disrupted
items.s: Microsoft says it is seeing some “positive results” as it works to restore services for millions of customers, after a disruption that began on Thursday evening GMT and has lasted more than 18 hours.
p: The disruption began around 6pm GMT on Thursday and has affected key Microsoft services, including Outlook, Teams and Copilot. It first hit mainly US users before spreading across the Asia-Pacific region, according to the Guardian’s live coverage.

Microsoft has suggested the outage may stem from settings applied to servers that keep Microsoft 365 running. The company said it does not believe it is suffering a cyber attack. It also admitted that a fix was “not taking as expected”.

Government agencies in Australia, Japan and the United States were reported to be affected, as were companies including OpenAI and Anthropic. Japan’s economy, trade and industry minister said the disruption had a “major impact” on the country’s economy.

Australia’s spy agency and federal police were among the organisations reporting disruption there. The coverage also cites a prediction of billions of dollars in damage, but the source of that figure is not named.

Microsoft’s latest update says it is seeing improved server stability after applying a software patch. Even so, the company still reports service degradation across its Microsoft 365 business and enterprise products and its consumer products.
items.cav: This account rests on a single live blog that is still being updated, so the situation may have changed since publication. The cause is only suggested by Microsoft and is not confirmed, and the billions-of-dollars estimate is unattributed. The sources do not say when full service will return.
items.op: A failure of this reach, hitting government agencies and public bodies, is a matter of public interest, not just a corporate inconvenience. Microsoft should give a clear and timely account of what went wrong with its server settings and how it will prevent a repeat. Vague talk of “stability” is not enough for customers and governments that depend on these systems.

items.t: Kallas warns EU against accepting Russia’s proposed sequence for Ukraine talks
items.s: EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has urged Europe not to agree to Russia’s proposed order of steps for negotiations on Ukraine. She argued that the bloc should keep to its existing position and insisted it must have a say in who represents it.
p: EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas has warned against the bloc agreeing to Russia’s proposed sequence of talks on Ukraine, according to remarks reported in The Guardian’s live coverage from Europe.

Kallas said the sequence would allow Moscow to “divert the attention away” from its actions and could leave Europe in a worse position. She said the EU had agreed that a ceasefire should come first, followed by a peace agreement, and only then any other talks.

She cautioned that Europeans risked “walking into the traps that Russia is setting”, pointing to what she described as the absence of a ceasefire. If discussions moved to the European security architecture before that, she said, the bloc would not be better off but worse off.

Kallas also welcomed what she described as the United States finally acknowledging that any deal between Russia and Ukraine requires Europeans, a point she said she had made about a year and a half earlier. She said she hoped Europe would not simply sit at the table but would really influence the outcome.

On the question of representation, Kallas said she wanted to be part of the EU negotiating team, noting she had been appointed to represent Europe on foreign and security policy. She said she would not be “representing myself” but would be bound by any mandate from the 27 member states.

Asked why Moscow did not want her involved, Kallas said Russia wanted no strong counterpart so it could push its maximum demands. She described Russia’s approach as issuing threats and ultimatums, using force, and then waiting for Western concessions, adding that Moscow goes “further” each time.
Kallas also criticised the United States for sending negotiators without an institutional role, saying the EU should not copy that pattern and should rely on its established institutions.
items.cav: The report comes from a live blog and relies on Kallas’s own account, with the quotes reported as spoken. The coverage does not give a Russian response, and the proposed sequence itself is not described in detail. Her claims about the US position and the mandate of the EU negotiator are her own assertions.
items.op: Talks on a war of aggression should be judged by whether they restore a ceasefire and protect the victim, not by the order the aggressor prefers. Europe should hold to the sequence it has already agreed and insist that its negotiator answers to 27 governments, not to whoever is convenient.

items.t: Microsoft outage disrupts NHS, police, courts and schools across the UK
items.s: Hospitals, GP surgeries, police forces and schools across the UK were hit by a global Microsoft outage that began late on Thursday, according to The Guardian. Services were still trying to restore systems on Friday morning.
p: Public services scrambled to recover as the outage caused what officials described as “widespread” and “serious” problems for the NHS. With email and other IT tools used in healthcare out of reach, some staff reportedly fell back on paper patient notes. Some employees could still open Microsoft Teams on their phones, but many meetings had to be called off.

An NHS England spokesperson said local services were using established methods to manage IT failures, such as other systems or paper records, so that urgent care and appointments could go ahead. The GMB union’s national secretary, Rachel Harrison, said ambulance and NHS trusts were badly affected, though emergency and life-threatening calls did not appear to be hit. Pharmacists warned that some prescriptions could be delayed because pharmacies struggled to contact GP practices and patients.

The effects spread well beyond health care. Some criminal trials were disrupted, with jurors sent home early and some prisoners not brought to court. A judge at Minshull Street crown court in Manchester said staff had been searching for a fax machine that morning. National Rail cautioned passengers that emailed tickets might be hard to reach and suggested they log into the booking website or app before travelling. The Metropolitan Police and other forces said the outage was limiting the ability to report crimes online, and Ofsted said it could not receive emails. Universities, which rely heavily on Outlook and other Microsoft tools, were expected to be among the worst affected.

Charles Lamanna, a Microsoft executive vice-president, said the outage did not appear to stem from a cyber-attack. Later on Friday the company said it was seeing early improvement and that email traffic was slowly returning. Downing Street said it was trying to get a complete understanding of the situation and asked the public to use other channels where services were down. It would not say whether its own offices had been affected, but said backup arrangements were in place.

The Bank of England and the Financial Conduct Authority were also caught up in the Outlook problems, yet a Bank spokesperson insisted that all critical operations were running as normal. Luke Pollard, the minister for defence readiness and industry, argued that the incident showed the country needed stronger protection against technology failures, pointing out that people now depend heavily on digital systems.
items.cav: This account rests on one outlet’s live reporting, and the situation was still changing when it was written. Claims about ambulance services and the wider economic impact are reports or warnings rather than confirmed measurements, and the full scale of the disruption is not stated.
items.op: A single vendor’s failure should not be able to stop hospitals, courts and police from doing their basic work. Public bodies that depend on one platform owe the public clear contingency plans and a published account of what failed. Ministers should demand that account from Microsoft and from their own departments.

items.t: UK GPs, police, pharmacies and Parliament hit by global Microsoft outage
items.s: Health services, police forces, schools and councils across the UK have been affected by a global Microsoft outage that is disrupting Outlook, Teams and Copilot. Microsoft says services are gradually being restored, but the full impact remains unclear.
p: NHS England told patients to keep their appointments unless they were told otherwise, while several large police forces urged the public to phone them if they wanted to report a crime. Schools, councils and some GP surgeries have also been affected, and some practices in Hampshire and Shropshire asked patients with urgent needs to phone or visit in person rather than use online messaging.

According to Microsoft, a problem caused by higher-than-usual stress on its servers led to the disruption. The company said services were now being restored gradually around the world, but users could still experience problems. Microsoft and cyber-security experts have ruled out a cyber-attack as the cause.

The government said it was working closely with the company to assess the impact on its own services. Downing Street said it was seeking a fuller picture of the effect on government departments. Local authorities warned that some council services were being disrupted, although the Local Government Association said plans were in place to keep support running.

The GMB union’s national secretary, Rachel Harrison, said the outage was having a serious impact on ambulance and NHS trusts. She said staff working in the 111 and 999 services were unable to refer patient details in the normal way, creating a large backlog, though emergency and life-threatening call-outs appeared unaffected.

Reports of wider health effects are not yet confirmed. There are anecdotal reports of caesarean sections being cancelled and of hospitals accepting only urgent referrals, but the impact on planned treatment has not been verified. The NHS calendar relies heavily on the Microsoft system, and working practices differ between hospitals and trusts, which makes the overall picture hard to judge.

The disruption has spread well beyond healthcare. Some teachers said they could not reach their calendars, emails or files, and parents in parts of Scotland were asked to phone in absences. Royal Mail said some online services were unavailable, though post was still being collected and delivered. MPs were unable to access their parliamentary accounts, and MSPs confirmed that Holyrood’s email systems were down. Some businesses have switched to paper or to messaging apps such as WhatsApp.

A cyber-security adviser at ESET, Jake Moore, compared the failure to a blocked motorway lane, in which traffic is forced onto the remaining lanes until everything slows. The companies involved have not yet said how long full restoration will take.
items.cav: The full extent of the disruption and the restoration timeline are not yet known. The reports of cancelled caesarean sections are anecdotal and unconfirmed, and the cause given by Microsoft has not been independently verified.
items.op: When one private platform underpins hospital scheduling, police reporting and parliamentary email, the public has a right to know who is accountable and how quickly it will be fixed. Governments that depend on a single supplier for critical services should publish their contingency plans, not just reassurances. Transparency about that dependency matters more than the outage itself.

items.t: Ukraine talks stall as Moscow widens the debate to Europe’s security order
items.s: Diplomacy over Ukraine has produced little so far, and according to Euronews the Kremlin is now pressing for a broader settlement covering the continent’s security. Ukrainian and Estonian leaders have questioned whether that discussion should come first.
p: Euronews reports that Kyiv had pushed for a European role in the Abu Dhabi negotiations, but the discussion has since moved to who should speak for Europe and how the continent’s security will be organised. After Abu Dhabi, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner flew on to Moscow to see Vladimir Putin, then travelled to Dublin to meet Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The Abu Dhabi round yielded a provisional accord on a large prisoner swap, but nothing firm on a truce or on territory. Speaking to Euronews’ Shona Murray after meeting the envoys, Zelenskyy said the timing and manner of the war’s end would shape every later step, and that those steps should follow the end of fighting and guarantees for Ukraine. He also argued that Ukraine already forms part of Europe’s security structure, and that NATO membership, if it came, would define one shared framework.

In Dublin, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said that discussing European security before a peace deal was a trap that played into Putin’s hands. He urged continued European backing for Ukraine and more pressure on Russia, especially as Moscow steps up strikes on energy and civilian infrastructure ahead of winter.

Russia’s chief negotiator, Vladimir Medinsky, told Russian state television on 11 November that the moment called for a new great-power settlement, comparable to the Yalta and Potsdam conferences. He said a fair security system could keep the peace for decades, provided it met Russia’s demands. The following day, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said Moscow expected the envoys to pass Putin’s messages to Zelenskyy in full, and that contacts would continue before a planned meeting between Putin and Donald Trump in China.

Moscow is also pressing for a three-way meeting with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, held alongside the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen on 18 to 19 November. Those arrangements have not been confirmed. Before the Abu Dhabi talks, an unnamed senior US official said both sides had privately shown some flexibility on disputed territory. Trump suggested Ukraine might emerge from the war in a different shape, but did not say what he meant.

Medinsky’s comments after the talks, however, indicated that Moscow’s stance had not moved. He ruled out swapping Russian-held areas along the border, rejected giving back occupied land, and said Russia would be satisfied only once it won and signed a deal on its own terms.
Euronews warns that the wider debate could let Moscow revive its long-standing demands over Ukraine and strengthen its hand before the China talks.
items.cav: The account rests on a single outlet’s reporting. The “flexibility” remark comes from an unnamed US official, and Trump’s comment is vague. The proposed China meeting is unconfirmed, and the warning about Moscow’s tactics is Euronews’ own assessment.
items.op: Europe should not let a debate about its future order replace the work of ending the fighting and securing guarantees for Ukraine. A settlement shaped around Moscow’s demands would reward the invasion. Transparency about who sits at the table and on what terms is the real test of any deal.

items.t: Global Microsoft 365 outage persists as Microsoft reports only partial recovery
items.s: Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and Copilot, were still disrupted more than 12 hours into a global outage, and the company described its progress as “marginal success”, according to Al Jazeera. The BBC reported that Microsoft has ruled out a cyber-attack.
p: Trouble started on Thursday afternoon GMT, when people began telling the outage tracker Downdetector that they could not reach Outlook, according to Al Jazeera. Within roughly sixty minutes, complaints had come in from 74 countries and territories. Microsoft first pointed to problems in the Americas, then acknowledged that users in any region could be affected.

The symptoms varied from one user to the next. Many people could not send or collect emails, open certain files or check their calendars, while others were able to chat and join video calls on Teams without difficulty. The BBC, citing Microsoft’s website, said Microsoft 365 is used by more than 430 million people.

The fallout has spread well beyond the software itself. The BBC reported that GP practices, pharmacies, police forces and schools across the UK were affected, and some surgeries asked patients not to send messages through their websites. In Toronto, a healthcare network running several hospitals reported email failures but said patient care was unaffected, according to CBC as relayed by the BBC. Al Jazeera said government systems in Singapore and Japan were disrupted, that the Supreme Court of the Philippines lost some communications, and that Australia’s intelligence agency and federal police were among those hit. OpenAI and Anthropic also said they had experienced problems.

Microsoft says the incident was not a cyber-security attack. It blames “elevated load” on its infrastructure, a state in which many servers drop offline and push their work onto those still running, straining them. Al Jazeera, however, reports that Microsoft said the load had not come from a rise in traffic, a point on which the two accounts differ. Microsoft has yet to publish a root cause, and on Friday it was rolling back a network change without confirming that the change was responsible.

Australia’s Home Affairs Minister, Tony Burke, said Microsoft had told him it did not believe a cyberattack was involved. He likened the situation in some respects to the CrowdStrike incident, in which a faulty update caused widespread disruption. Analysts quoted by Al Jazeera put forward a flawed internal update as one plausible cause, along with physical damage to infrastructure or errors in automated systems, but said the evidence so far was limited.

Estimates of the scale are uncertain. The BBC cited 140,000 Downdetector reports from 74 countries on Thursday evening, while Al Jazeera counted at least 43,000 reports from 72 countries around 07:00 GMT on Friday. Both outlets note that the tracker depends on people choosing to file reports, so the number actually affected is likely much higher.

On Friday afternoon, Microsoft said it had made encouraging progress toward recovery in Europe and improvement in North America. It warned that some users could still experience intermittent problems while the remaining areas of disruption are addressed.
items.cav: The sources do not confirm the root cause, and Microsoft’s explanation has not been independently verified. The outlets report different Downdetector figures from different times, and they describe the traffic question differently. The analyst comments are opinion and speculation rather than findings.
items.op: One company’s failure has halted email and collaboration tools for governments, hospitals and police. Microsoft should publish a full root-cause report with a clear timeline, so customers can judge whether such failures can be prevented. Dependence on a single provider is a public concern, and transparency is the least that those who relied on it are owed.

items.t: Microsoft races to restore Teams and Outlook after global outage hits users worldwide
items.s: Microsoft is working to fix an outage that disrupted Teams, Outlook and other services across the globe for more than 12 hours. The company says it is seeing early signs of recovery but has not yet explained the root cause.
p: The outage affected millions of users across Thursday and Friday. In an update, the company said it was seeing “early signs of stabilisation” as it worked to increase capacity so more users could get back on its systems. Microsoft said recovery actions had been completed across portions of the affected infrastructure in the Asia Pacific region, and that traffic was being gradually restored, with improvements in mailbox access and delayed email processing. It warned that some users may still face intermittent problems.

The problem appeared uneven, with some but not all users reporting failures. The outage monitoring site Down Detector recorded nearly 130,000 reports from 74 countries on Thursday evening, covering Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive and Copilot. Microsoft said more than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps.

Microsoft said there were no indications that a cyber-attack caused the failure. It said a number of servers were “unexpectedly unavailable” after they failed automated checks, and that a portion of its infrastructure was experiencing elevated load. The company has suggested that settings applied to servers supporting Microsoft 365 may be to blame, but it has not confirmed this. It promised a post-incident report with full details of the root cause once the problem is mitigated.

The effects spread well beyond office software. In the UK, pharmacies reported difficulties contacting some GP surgeries about prescriptions, causing what the report describes as significant waiting times for medicines. Several police forces asked people not to report crimes online and to phone instead, and some schools told parents that email and Teams were down. National Rail warned that passengers might not be able to access emailed tickets. The UK government said it was “working closely” with Microsoft to assess the impact on government services.

Businesses elsewhere were also hit. Indian airlines IndiGo and Akasa Air reported problems with email support. Taiwanese security firms, life insurers and investment trust companies said fund management services had been disrupted. In Japan, a shipping company said it could not take online reservations for some services, and a pharmaceutical firm said it was handling orders by phone.

Mark Gregory, an associate professor at RMIT University in Melbourne, said the failure appeared to involve the network layer and could resemble a configuration fault that disrupted Optus’s network in 2023. He described how a loss of servers can overload the remaining ones, creating a cascade. His comments are an outside view and not a confirmed diagnosis. Microsoft also reported an Azure cloud outage last month.
items.cav: The cause has not been confirmed. The suggested settings problem and the academic’s configuration theory are both unverified, and the full post-incident report has not yet been published. Figures such as the Down Detector reports and the Microsoft 365 user count come from the company or a monitoring site rather than an independent audit.
items.op: Millions of people and essential services depend on a few cloud platforms, so an outage becomes a public matter. Microsoft should publish its root-cause report promptly and in plain detail. Customers, hospitals and police need to know not only what failed but why the backup routes were not enough.

items.t: Microsoft reports early recovery after global outage disrupted Teams and Outlook
items.s: Microsoft says it is seeing early improvement after a worldwide disruption to its systems, which affected users of Teams and Outlook for more than 12 hours across Thursday and Friday, according to The Guardian’s First Thing newsletter.
p: According to the newsletter, the failure reached organisations and public bodies in several countries. The company described “early signs of stabilisation” after the disruption had lasted more than 12 hours, and the briefing says millions of users were affected.

Not every user was hit to the same degree. Some people reported difficulties with Microsoft Teams and with Outlook email, the summary says, though it does not set out which other services were down or for how long in each location.

The reach of the platforms helps explain the spread. Citing the company, the newsletter puts the number of people using Microsoft 365 apps at more than 430 million and says more than 90% of Fortune 500 companies use Copilot. These are Microsoft’s own figures, relayed second-hand, and they have not been independently checked in the material available.

Microsoft said it had seen no indications that a cyber-attack caused the failure. That position matters, because outages at large cloud providers often prompt concern about a wider breach. The source does not say what did trigger the disruption.

Readers following the recovery are directed to a live blog that the newsletter says is tracking the restoration work and the continuing impact. The material available does not give a restoration timetable or a total count of affected organisations.

The episode shows how many routine tasks, from messaging to meetings to email, now run through a small number of providers. When one platform fails, the disruption spreads quickly across unrelated parts of daily life. Recovery is welcome, but the question of how a single failure could reach so far remains open.
items.cav: The source is a short newsletter summary, so the root cause, the full list of affected services and the recovery timeline are not confirmed here. The “millions of users” figure and Microsoft’s usage statistics are second-hand and unverified.
items.op: Companies that run infrastructure this widely used owe customers a full account of what failed and why, not only assurances that things are getting better. The denial of a cyber-attack is useful, but it cannot replace a published explanation. Accountability begins once the systems are back, when the cause must finally be named.

items.t: Iran's Guards claim they destroyed US radar in Bahrain, a first direct attack in months
items.s: Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps says it hit a US early-warning radar in Bahrain, its first direct attack on US military installations for months. The claim comes as Washington and Tehran's diplomatic channels remain open but strained.
p: On Friday, Iran's Revolutionary Guard said its forces had hit a US early-warning radar in Bahrain, according to state media. The Guard presented the operation as retaliation for an attack on a communications tower in Sirik, in southern Iran, a site that looks out over the Strait of Hormuz.

The Guardian reported that the Sirik tower was struck by a US airstrike, a version that follows the IRGC's account. Euronews said only that the tower was attacked on Thursday and did not say who carried out the attack. Neither outlet offers an independent account of the radar strike, and no US military response to the Guard's claim appears in the material available.

In a statement, the Guard described its move as a "serious warning" to Washington. It told the United States to stop what it called airborne provocations and smuggling of oil through the strait, and said its aerospace force was ready to act anywhere if similar incidents recurred.

Bahrain is home to the headquarters of the US Navy's Fifth Fleet, a force central to American naval activity in the Gulf. US Central Command said on Wednesday that its forces were keeping the strait open to commercial traffic while enforcing a naval blockade of Iran.

President Donald Trump has hardened his tone in recent days. He said he would strike Iran only if necessary and claimed that several Gulf states, Saudi Arabia among them, had urged him to hold off on large-scale attacks. He also asked Vice-President JD Vance to drop talks with Tehran and turn his attention to problems at home. Iran had seen Vance as the Trump adviser it could trust most, yet it turned down his request for a face-to-face meeting to discuss the terms of a peace deal.

Diplomacy has not stopped entirely. Qatar and Pakistan are still acting as mediators. Tehran, however, will only resume formal negotiations with Washington if its conditions are met, which include lifting sanctions, ending the blockade of its ports, unfreezing assets and stopping the fighting on every front.

Separately, Iran's Assembly of Experts, the clerical body that selects the supreme leader, issued a statement on Thursday calling for Iran's membership of the nuclear non-proliferation treaty to be reviewed. The Guardian described this as the first time a governing institution in Iran has pushed for such a review, and said it could pave the way for religious approval of a nuclear weapon. Whether Iran actually has the uranium or the technology to build one remains disputed. The UN nuclear watchdog has voiced alarm that it still lacks information about Iran's nuclear sites and access to the Isfahan facility.

A YouGov poll for the Council for Arab-British Understanding, taken on Tuesday and Wednesday, found that 65% of Britons would oppose the US resuming its war with Iran, while 14% would back it. On Thursday, a UK court found two Iranians guilty of spying and of planning attacks on journalists. The Iranian embassy said the verdict was an attempt to push a political agenda.
items.cav: The radar strike rests on IRGC and state media claims that the sources do not independently confirm. The sources also differ on who carried out the tower attack, and the US response is not reported.
items.op: Military claims of destroyed targets and a president's shifting signals about talks should not be left for the public to piece together. Any strike needs independent confirmation and a clear public justification, and a deal should not be traded away behind closed doors.

items.t: Microsoft Outlook, Teams and Copilot outage triggers wave of online jokes
items.s: A major Microsoft outage affecting Outlook, Teams and the Copilot service has been reported in more than 70 countries. Social media users have responded with jokes as the company works on a fix.
p: Microsoft is dealing with a major outage affecting its Outlook, Teams and Copilot services, according to Euronews. The disruption first began on Thursday, according to the monitoring website Downdetector, and has been reported in more than 70 countries.

Euronews says the outage is affecting millions of users globally, though the article does not give a breakdown of how many people were affected in each country. Microsoft has continued to post updates. It said the changes meant to fix the problem are “not taking as expected,” and the article does not say when service might be fully restored.

Online reaction has been largely humorous. Microsoft became the top trending term on social media, and users shared posts joking about when Outlook might return, with some suggesting it could wait until January. Others sent messages of sympathy to the engineers working on the repair, urging them to rest.

One widely shared post claimed that Microsoft had announced that 25 per cent of its workforce would be made redundant. The article presents this only as a social media joke and does not confirm it with the company.
items.cav: The article relies on Downdetector data and social media posts rather than an official Microsoft account of the cause or the number of users affected. The workforce cut claim comes from a user post and is not verified in the source.
items.op: When a service used for email and meetings fails across more than 70 countries, users are left guessing about the cause and the timeline. Microsoft's updates say the fix is not yet working as planned, and that is not enough. The company should publish a fuller account of what failed and when service will return.

items.t: One dead and four injured in Washington DC gym shooting; suspect dies after standoff
items.s: A gunman opened fire inside a gym in a Washington DC apartment building on Thursday morning, killing one person and wounding four others before dying in an apartment after a standoff with police. Authorities are still working to establish the timeline and motive.
p: Police said one person was killed and four others were injured after the shooting, which began shortly before 8am local time at a VIDA Fitness gym in an apartment building in the Logan Circle area of Northwest Washington. The Guardian reported that the person who died was 46-year-old James Stuart, the building manager, though the BBC's report did not name the victim.

Officers were on the scene within 30 seconds of the report, police said. Interim police chief Jeffery Carroll told reporters that the suspect, later identified as 55-year-old Matt Wade Lambert, had left the gym and fired from an area outside, then barricaded himself in a seventh-floor apartment. Carroll said Lambert had three firearms and had broken a gas line and started a fire.

Negotiators spoke with the suspect for more than an hour. Carroll said they heard a gunshot and then officers forced their way into the apartment, where they found Lambert with what appeared to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound. The BBC reported that Lambert had fired through the door at officers at least twice while barricaded, a detail the Guardian did not include.

Court records cited by the Guardian show that Lambert had been in a civil dispute with the homeowners association of the building since March 2025. He alleged that his unit suffered mold, moisture and water damage after repairs to the building’s facade. The association denied negligence in court filings, and the case was still ongoing.

Police had earlier described a conflict between the shooter and the association. Carroll told reporters that police believed there was some sort of conflict with the apartment building but had little more than that. DC council member Brooke Pinto told Fox 5 DC that she believed the suspect went to the gym to target the building owner. That remains her belief and has not been confirmed by police.

Mayor Muriel Bowser called the shooting a senseless act of gun violence and said the White House had been briefed. Janeese Lewis George, the city’s mayor-elect, described the shooting as horrifying and expressed condolences to the victims and families.

A 23-year-old witness, Anthony Mirones, told the Guardian he was on a treadmill when he heard a loud bang and then saw a man dead on the floor. Another witness told the BBC that people hid behind planters and that a fire alarm was pulled. Both accounts describe the scene as chaotic, and details such as the number of shots differ between witnesses.

VIDA Fitness said its Logan Circle location was temporarily closed and would remain closed until further notice. Police said the scene was safe but asked the public to avoid the area while they cleared the building.
items.cav: Motive and timeline remain unconfirmed; the council member’s account of a targeted attack is a claim, not a police finding. The sources also differ on where the suspect fired from and whether the shots at officers were fired through the door.
items.op: A repair dispute over mold and water damage belongs in court or in negotiation, not in a gym full of people. Residents deserve a clear, verified timeline and motive, not claims passed along before investigators have finished their work.

items.t: Economists divided over Nvidia’s future after Jensen Huang steps down
items.s: Two economists speaking at Web Summit Lisbon disagreed on how lasting the damage will be after Nvidia’s chief executive stepped down. One called his exit a setback for the sector, while the other said large companies tend to outlast their leaders.
p: Jensen Huang stepped down on Thursday as chief executive of Nvidia, according to the coverage, after an affair involving an alleged Chinese spy and a company employee came to light. The reporting presents these allegations as claims, and the sources do not explain the evidence behind them. The departure has unsettled a market that leans heavily on a small group of major companies, although the commentators quoted do not expect lasting harm to Nvidia itself.

Speaking on a panel moderated by Euronews at Web Summit in Lisbon, investor Adam Kobeissi, who runs The Kobeissi Letter, described the move as a loss for the sector as a whole. He argued that more time should have been spent on an inquiry before Huang left, calling the decision “a critical mistake.”

James Galbraith, a professor at the Lyndon B. Johnson School of Public Affairs at the University of Texas at Austin, offered a calmer assessment. In his view, big firms are structured to continue beyond whoever leads them, and if Nvidia is as robust as its reputation suggests, the disruption may be short-lived.

Kobeissi was less sanguine about spillover effects. Because so much of the sector’s growth rests on a few firms, he said it was “hard to say” whether anything at Nvidia could be viewed in isolation. He also expects Anthropic to proceed with its public listing, possibly as early as next week.

He added that private debt has become “a little tapped out” as a source of funding, and that the coming quarters will be uncertain because of the midterm election result, shifts in policy and other pressures. He doubted that investors can simply wait for that uncertainty to fade.
The panellists’ predictions are opinions, and the sources offer no market data to test them.
items.cav: The affair and espionage claims are allegations reported in the coverage, and the sources do not say who made them public or what evidence supports them. The economists are commentators, and the Anthropic timing is one speaker’s expectation rather than a confirmed date.
items.op: When a chief executive leaves amid allegations that have not been tested, the public deserves to know what the investigation found and how the decision was reached. Markets can move on rumour, but accountability depends on transparent process. Investors should demand the facts before they treat the story as settled.

items.t: Israeli strike on Nasser hospital in Gaza kills six, including surgeon, officials say
items.s: An Israeli airstrike on Nasser hospital in Khan Younis killed six people, among them a surgeon, early on Thursday, according to the hospital director. The Israeli military says it was targeting a Hamas commander and other fighters inside the building.
p: The attack came shortly after midnight, at around 12.30am, according to Dr Ayman Abu Ubaid, a surgical specialist who was hurt in the bombing. He told the Guardian that the blast arrived with no prior notice, while the patients on his ward were awaiting operations and should have been asleep. Hospital director Dr Ahmed al-Fara put the toll at six dead and 28 wounded.

Among those killed was Rizk Abu Shaira, 52, a general surgeon who had been filmed working in the documentary American Doctor. He died together with one of the patients he had just operated on. Another victim, Seif Ghazi Abu Hatab, 29, had been brought in on Monday with a back injury sustained while he helped clear rubble from a friend’s house. He was due in theatre on Thursday morning and was expected to travel abroad for further care.

Al-Fara said the explosion wrecked part of the surgical unit and damaged several floors. Radiology, laboratories, operating theatres and inpatient surgical wards have all been halted. Video and accounts from the scene show a collapsed ceiling, beds buried in debris and a gap torn through a floor where the munition came down. He added that the facility is already short of roughly 80% of its essential drugs and supplies.

The Israeli military stated that it had hit a Hamas commander and other militants at the site, but it did not provide evidence to back that claim. Israel has previously argued that Hamas uses hospitals as command posts and weapons depots. Hamas denies this.

Nasser is among the few healthcare facilities still working in Gaza. According to the Guardian, it has come under attack seven times since the war began, and a strike last year on the site killed five journalists. Doctors Without Borders says Israel has detained hundreds of medics since October 2023, at least 95 of them still held. UN experts have called the wider destruction of the territory’s health system “medicide”.

France 24 reports that Israeli fire killed 11 people across Gaza on Thursday, with six of those deaths coming from the Nasser strike, and describes it as the deadliest single attack since Israel’s elections last month. Gaza’s health ministry says more than 1,600 people have been killed by Israeli strikes since the October 2025 ceasefire.

International humanitarian law prohibits attacks on medical facilities and personnel. A hospital may lose that protection if it is being used for military purposes, but the reports so far do not establish that this was the case here.
items.cav: The sources give different wounded figures: the hospital director says 28, while the Guardian’s video summary refers to more than 20. The military’s claim about a Hamas commander is unsupported by any evidence in the reports, and the casualty numbers come mostly from hospital and health officials that could not be independently verified here.
items.op: A hospital is supposed to be the one place where the sick and wounded are safe from fighting, yet a strike that kills a surgeon mid-treatment tests that principle. If the military believes Hamas fighters were inside, it should publish the evidence it has so far withheld. Unproven claims cannot justify the deaths of doctors and patients.

items.t: Infant dies of cold in Gaza tent as aid limits and floods deepen displaced families' hardship
items.s: A nine-month-old Palestinian boy has died of cold in a tent in southern Gaza, according to his father and a doctor. The death came as Israel is said to be restricting winter supplies, and as floods have compounded the plight of people living in temporary shelters.
p: A baby boy has died of exposure in a family tent in southern Gaza, where his displaced relatives were sheltering, according to his father and a medical source. The death is unfolding while Israel is reported to be keeping tight limits on winter aid entering the territory, which has been devastated by war.
A doctor, who asked not to be named, told the AFP news agency on Thursday that nine-month-old Kinan Ahmed Raqiq died from hypothermia in Khan Younis.

The child's father, Ahmed Raqiq, told AFP that the temperature fell sharply overnight. He said he found the boy's skin had turned blue and took him to Nasser Hospital, where doctors found he had already died. Speaking outside the hospital, he said he was “in complete shock.”
Mahmoud Basal, the spokesman for Gaza's Civil Defence, confirmed the death was caused by extreme cold, the Palestinian outlet Al-Quds reported.

The United Kingdom, Qatar and Jordan lead a coalition of more than 50 countries and organisations. They have urged Israel to let in shelter materials, fuel, water, sanitation and medical supplies without delay, warning that many people in Gaza still lack adequate housing and face risks such as hypothermia and chest infections.

Israel's caretaker Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has rejected the criticism. He said Israel had allowed in 91,000 tents and blamed Hamas alone for the suffering of Gaza's population. The source material does not explain how these figures were checked.

Heavy rain this week flooded camps and damaged tens of thousands of tents. Five people, three of them children, were killed the day after the flooding, when a sandy embankment gave way and fell onto their shelters. The UN humanitarian coordination office, OCHA, said 26,000 households had been hit by storms as of November 8. It also estimated that about 65 percent of Gaza's population remains displaced in tents or other temporary shelter.
James Elder, a UNICEF spokesman on Gaza, said the flooding was only a foretaste of the cold season, stressing that winter has not yet arrived.
items.cav: The cause of death rests on the father's account and an anonymous doctor's statement; the evidence includes no post-mortem or official medical report. The Civil Defence confirmation is second-hand, relayed through Al-Quds, and Netanyahu's claims about tent numbers are not independently verified in the source material.
items.op: Shelter and fuel are not political bargaining chips, and a child freezing in a tent is the clearest sign of what delay costs. Israel should open verifiable channels for supplies now and publish the delivery figures behind its claims. Without that transparency, neither side's account can be tested, and the families paying the price will keep waiting.

items.t: Eight dead as three-storey Brooklyn building collapses into neighbouring construction pit
items.s: Eight people have died and 18 others were hurt after a three-storey residential building gave way in Brooklyn's Flatbush neighbourhood on Wednesday. Officials are examining whether criminal charges could follow.
p: Witnesses told the BBC they heard a sudden, deafening bang and saw a cloud of dust rise as the structure gave way. Part of it tumbled into an excavation site next door, where workers were on duty at the time. The 1930s building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue held apartments and a shop on its ground level.

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said some workers, themselves narrowly spared, went back to the wreckage and pulled victims out from under the debris. Fire Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said crews reached the scene within minutes and described their conduct as “incredibly heroic”. She added that the search would carry on until no one remained unaccounted for, even though heavy rain and cold weather hampered work at the site.

Authorities put the death toll at eight, comprising six adults and two children, with two of the dead being construction workers. Mamdani said six people were declared dead where the building fell, and two more died later in hospital. Four of the injured are firefighters, and one patient is still in hospital in critical condition.

Residents were living in the building when it fell. On the neighbouring plot, excavation was under way for a project that has already received approval, featuring 64 homes and a supermarket on its lower floor. CBS News reported that it remains unclear whether that digging had any bearing on the collapse.

The Ecuadorian consul general visited the area and confirmed that two of the victims are Ecuadorian citizens, according to the New York Times. Gicela Andrade told the newspaper that one of them, Jose Luis Caguana Cosquillo, is to be flown home for burial. She named the other victim as Gabriel Ariolfo Siguencia.

Investigators say the developers hold live permits for excavation and foundation work connected to the new project, and have named the developer as Robert Fischman. Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez wrote on X that his office is working with the Department of Buildings and other law enforcement partners to establish whether any criminal conduct played a part. Mamdani said every party tied to the building and the site would be scrutinised and made answerable.

On Thursday, Department of Buildings head Ahmed Tigani told a news conference that no code violations had been logged for the property before the collapse. He said the developer is linked to at least 100 other locations across the city, and all of them are now being reviewed. More than 250 firefighters came out and worked through the night to locate those trapped. Forecasters were predicting heavy rain across the New York region later the same day.
items.cav: The cause of the collapse is not yet established, and officials have not linked it to the adjacent excavation. The Ecuadorian nationality of two victims and the burial plans come from the consul and a New York Times report rather than an official statement. The death toll is consistent across accounts, but the number of injured and their condition may change.
items.op: When a residential building falls into a site where people are working, the public is owed a clear account of who approved what and who checked it. Permits, inspections and developer ties across 100 sites must be examined in the open, not deferred to a process that promises accountability later. The families of the dead deserve answers before the rubble is cleared.

items.t: Jensen Huang's exit from Nvidia: an opinion on why the board had to act
items.s: Nvidia's chief executive Jensen Huang has resigned after confessing to an affair, and a Guardian columnist argues the board was right to remove him despite his reputation as irreplaceable. The column draws on reports and comment rather than new disclosures.
p: Nvidia’s co-founder Jensen Huang has stepped down as chief executive, after confessing to an extramarital affair. According to the Guardian column by Nils Pratley, many commentators had described him as “irreplaceable” at the start of the week, arguing that the chipmaker would struggle without his leadership.

The affair at the centre of the case involved Alice Huang, who is not related to him and who is the head of Megaspeed, a Singapore-based firm. The column notes that the firm is suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips into China. It also says US officials regard Alice Huang as a Chinese spy. The column does not say whether Jensen Huang knew of that view.

Reports of a second affair, this time with a senior Nvidia employee, added to the pressure, the column says. It argues that the board may also have been concerned about what further material could emerge in the coming weeks.

Nvidia’s shares fell sharply after the announcement. The column reports an initial drop of 13 per cent, which later narrowed to about 5 per cent as investors weighed the company’s strong position in the market for graphics processing units. The analyst Dan Ives is quoted as backing the change of leadership.

Pratley gives three main reasons for the board’s decision. First, congressional investigations are expected regardless. Democratic senators have asked administration officials to preserve documents on the sale of Nvidia’s advanced chips to China, and the company’s ties to the Trump administration are likely to face closer scrutiny. Second, Huang’s credibility as an advocate for looser export restrictions has been undermined. Third, the column argues that the company had relied too heavily on one individual, and that its board had not addressed this.

To manage the transition, Colette Kress, the chief financial officer, will serve as interim chief executive. Harvey Jones, a former chief executive of the semiconductor company Synopsys and a current director, is to become independent chair. The column suggests that further governance changes, possibly including new independent directors, may follow.

The column acknowledges that the management task will be difficult and that the political climate in Washington has changed. Its central argument is that a company of Nvidia’s size could not justify keeping a leader whose position had been compromised.
items.cav: This is an opinion column, and several key claims are presented as reports or as the views of US officials rather than established facts. The column does not confirm that Jensen Huang knew of Alice Huang’s reported status, and the allegations about Megaspeed and the second affair are not verified in the piece. The share price figures are as stated in the column and may have changed since.
items.op: Boards owe shareholders candour, and Nvidia’s case shows that governance cannot rest on one star executive. Congressional scrutiny of chip exports to China is legitimate and should proceed in full view. The directors were right to act, but the real test is whether they build checks that outlast any single chief executive.

items.t: Russia downplays US hopes of a European seat at Ukraine peace talks
items.s: Moscow has played down US envoys’ suggestion that Vladimir Putin will accept a European presence in negotiations to end the war in Ukraine. Instead, Russia has asked Europe to stop military aid to Kyiv first.
p: US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner had suggested that Putin agreed to a European presence in the talks. According to the source, Russia has downplayed those comments and set a condition: Europe should cease military aid to Ukraine.

Witkoff and Kushner flew to Moscow to seek Putin’s consent for Europeans to join a multilateral format. So far, the process has run between Ukraine and Russia, with US moderation. The trip followed two days of negotiations in Abu Dhabi, where the Russian delegation declined to sit down with the European team.

Witkoff told reporters, citing Reuters, that Europeans would join the next meeting. He called this an important moment because they are Russia’s partners as well. Kushner described the discussions as detailed and said they would hopefully feed into a multilateral format.

Putin’s aide, Yuri Ushakov, cautioned against seating Russians and Europeans at the same table. He said Europeans first needed to choose between “peace” and “war”, a reference to their military support for Ukraine. Ushakov argued that Europe’s practical actions pointed toward the latter.

The source reports that Putin wants to revise the continent’s security architecture. Europeans, it says, see that topic as a way to divert attention from the war and to advance Russian great-power aims, including veto power over NATO’s future membership. Putin cited Donald Trump’s plan for a broad agreement that might involve all of Europe.

Putin’s response to European leaders, reported by the source, was that they should talk only after there is peace in Ukraine. He then accused them of planning to deploy troops into Ukrainian territory once fighting ended. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and High Representative Kaja Kallas have both made security talks conditional on a ceasefire.

In Dublin, European leaders rejected Putin’s approach. They argued that Moscow had breached security agreements that had been in place for decades, and that any discussion of the architecture required a European presence. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said it was important that Russia come to the table. EU leaders were due to discuss appointing a special envoy, which Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has requested by the end of the month. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said such a designation was a prerequisite for joining the talks.

The peace process has so far produced limited progress beyond prisoner swaps, according to the source. Russia also left room for some contact: last month Putin held a 90-minute phone call with the leaders of Finland and Norway.
items.cav: The US envoys’ account that Putin accepts a European role is not confirmed by Moscow, which has downplayed it. Witkoff’s remarks come via Reuters as reported by Euronews, and the Dublin position is described only in summary. Peskov’s remarks are quoted through the source without a fuller readout.
items.op: A settlement that excludes the countries that must guarantee and police it invites a deal Europe cannot honour. Moscow’s demand that aid stop before talks begin turns a security question into a bargaining chip. Negotiators should publish their terms and insist that Europe has a seat.
